title: Model routing: test whether Jev adds value
affiliation: TokenTrim; external author; not independently reproduced here.
workload: Select a model for a user query.
method: Author reports offline scoring on 5,835 held-out LLMRouterBench queries across 13 models; answers are precomputed.
baseline: Best fixed model and identical retrieval router without Jev.
finding: Retrieval routing improved the frontier, but the no-Jev ablation matched it. This does not establish that the Jev difficulty signal caused savings.
limitations: Cached downstream answers; no live end-to-end answer latency. Reported cost uses benchmark assumptions.
implication: Before adding a model router, compare a fixed default and a no-Jev retrieval policy. Ship a router only if the added signal earns its overhead.
headline: No-Jev ablation matched the hybrid frontier.

title: Choosing tools from real MCP inventories
affiliation: BillionsBobby/JevRouter; external project author; not rerun here.
workload: Predict the first five tool calls for Toolathlon tasks.
method: Ten tasks; inventories from nine live MCP servers. Serial and decomposed Jev routing compared with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.
baseline: DeepSeek tool predictions; serial versus decomposed Jev.
finding: Serial Jev was faster in this report; decomposition increased position-wise matches but also increased latency.
limitations: Only ten tasks and predicted sequences; this is not demonstrated task completion. Provider, prompts and mode affect the tradeoff.
implication: Offer a next-tool recommendation over explicit candidates. Do not market a predicted multi-step sequence as a reliable autonomous plan.
metrics: Position-wise hits: serial Jev 38%, decomposed 44%, DeepSeek 24%.
headline: Better tool prediction can still take longer.

title: Separate questions for separate hazards
affiliation: AnshChoudhary; external project author; not rerun here.
workload: Flag hazards in proposed agent tool calls before execution.
method: 600 authored records, 320 held out; full hazard battery compared with a broad dangerousness question.
finding: Decomposed questions sharply reduced false blocks on hard negatives in this corpus. Calibration and latency targets still failed.
limitations: Author-designed synthetic attacks are not evidence of adversarial security in production. Approval friction must be measured separately.
implication: Use independent, explicit checks as advisory signals. Keep authorization, execution safeguards and human approval outside Jev.
metrics: Hard-negative block rate: full battery 0%; generic question 39.2%.
headline: Explicit checks helped; calibration and latency limits remain.

title: Log triage: filtering is not automatically saving
affiliation: Jalil Laaraichi / jevlogs; same maintainer as System One Engine.
workload: Select log records for deeper analysis while preserving originals.
method: 2,500 HDFS and 2,500 BGL records; threshold, severity, cache and rule comparisons. Existing results inspected; no new rerun.
finding: The conservative HDFS policy sent nearly everything for analysis. The modeled downstream bill increased rather than decreased. BGL recall was explained by deterministic FATAL protection.
limitations: HDFS labels are block-level, not true line-level incident labels. The cost example assumes downstream token counts and prices, not actual billing. Upstream Loghub data has research/academic terms.
implication: Expose triage alongside exact reuse and visible bypass rates. Compare simple severity rules first; never sell universal savings or discard original records.
metrics: HDFS anomaly recall 99.33%; only 0.84% routed away from deeper analysis.
headline: Conservative triage can add cost; reuse may help more.

title: Navigating beyond a flat choice limit
affiliation: Jalil Laaraichi / jev-tree; same maintainer as System One Engine.
workload: Classify an incident into one of 320 authored categories.
method: 180 synthetic cases; authored tree, automatic partitioning, truncated flat choice and keyword baseline. Existing recorded results inspected.
baseline: Deterministic keyword extraction and first-255 truncation.
finding: Hierarchical selection reached categories excluded by truncation. The deterministic parser also solved every case, so this is evidence about taxonomy coverage, not a need for AI.
limitations: Synthetic fields are easy to parse. Accuracy is not evidence of production robustness or calibrated confidence. Three tree steps add calls.
implication: Use semantic categories when a flat list is too large. First check whether structured input already identifies the answer without inference.
metrics: Truncation: 90/180; keyword baseline: 180/180 with zero model calls.
headline: Trees avoid truncation; structured data may need no model.

title: Typed evaluation versus chat-model wrappers
affiliation: TypeSafe AI, the Jev model vendor; not independently reproduced here.
workload: Bounded decisions inside four application workflows.
method: Vendor launch comparison of typed Jev evaluations and chat-model decision wrappers.
finding: The launch report supports evaluating typed decisions as a separate operation. Its headline speed and cost ratios are vendor-specific workload results.
limitations: Vendor-authored comparison, selected tasks and wrappers. Reported ratios do not predict a coding agent’s total cost or time. Pricing and Gateway promotions change.
implication: Batch independent questions over shared evidence. Measure host tool overhead and final outcomes before promising savings.
metrics: Vendor advertises up to 193.6× speed and 444.6× cost improvements in its evaluation; not System One Engine results.
headline: A reason to test typed decisions, not a savings guarantee.

title: Define ambiguity before evaluating a workflow
affiliation: Vercel; platform guidance, not an independent benchmark.
workload: Classification and routing where outcomes and review behavior can be specified.
method: Official examples and design guidance; no qualifying comparative run in this record.
baseline: A deterministic rule or direct reasoning in the host should remain a candidate.
finding: Clear output choices and an explicit ambiguity policy make an evaluation meaningful.
limitations: Documentation examples do not establish a measured accuracy or savings rate.
implication: Provide reusable recipes with explicit review paths. Distinguish a prompt design problem from a model failure.
headline: Specify what uncertain and mixed cases should do.

title: Batching two evidence checks
affiliation: System One Bench / Jalil Laaraichi; same maintainer as System One Engine.
workload: Check whether short tool evidence supports or explicitly contradicts a claim.
method: 12 authored cases, 24 labels; batch versus two sequential SDK requests; alternating order, no cache or retries. Labels and corpus hash precede the first run. Live Jev via Vercel Gateway.
baseline: The same questions in separate sequential requests; no expensive host-model comparison.
finding: Batching reduced calls, input tokens and median case latency, with one additional incorrect answer in this small run.
limitations: Tiny synthetic diagnostic, not a held-out production benchmark. No host-agent tool overhead, final task success or invoice savings measured. One run is not a stable latency distribution.
implication: Batch independent checks when evidence is shared, but evaluate quality as well as request count. Preserve uncertainty and inspect contradictions rather than blindly accepting the cheaper configuration.
metrics: Batch: 23/24 labels correct; 12 calls; 4,113 input tokens; case p50 256ms, p95 535ms.
Separate: 24/24 correct; 24 calls; 7,530 input tokens; case p50 537ms, p95 685ms.
Both modes flagged 3/24 answers for review; zero failed requests.
headline: Fewer calls and tokens, with one extra error in this small test.
